title: Bhai Nand Lal
hookLine: a Persian poet and scholar who served at Guru Gobind Singh's court

lines: A LATER COURT, A NEW LANGUAGE.
cards: Bhai Gurdas has been our guide since this year began, writing in Punjabi and in Braj, close to the Gurus who came before. Now the path hands us to a second teller, from a later court and a different language.
He's a learned man who writes in Persian, the language Rumi and Hafiz wrote in, and he spends his gift on Guru Gobind Singh. Sikhs know him by a title of respect, and by a pen name. Today: Goya.

teach.h: A POET AND SCHOLAR AT COURT.
teach.b: Bhai Nand Lal was a poet and a scholar who served at the court of Guru Gobind Singh. Bhai is the same title of respect Bhai Gurdas carries: brother.
He wrote under a pen name, Goya, in the Persian manner, and what he wrote, he wrote in Persian. Here's the thing to notice.

teach.h: PERSIAN PICTURES, TURNED TO THE ONE.
teach.b: A court in his world was a place of learning and display, and Persian poetry was a high art, with its own rules, its own pictures, its own long tradition of writing about love for the Divine as a lover writes about the beloved.

Nand Lal didn't leave that behind when he came to the Guru. He didn't decide that a Sikh had to stop being a poet, or stop writing in the language he'd mastered. He turned the whole art toward the Guru.
The lover, the beloved, the beloved's face: in his poems, those old Persian pictures point to the One, and to the Guru who shows the way.
Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh gathered poets around him, and Nand Lal is one of the names Sikhs remember.

teach.h: LEARNING AS A WAY OF DEVOTION.
teach.b: His learning wasn't treated as a distraction from devotion. It became a way of devotion.
Over the next few days you'll meet some of his writing: a book about life, his love poems, and writings on conduct that carry his name.

Today, just meet the man: a scholar at court, a poet with a pen name, who brought the best thing he had, his Persian, and laid it at the Guru's feet. Sikh custom lets his poems, with Bhai Gurdas's vars, be sung in kirtan.

how: Sikhs read and sing Bhai Nand Lal's Persian poems, and Sikh custom allows them, with Bhai Gurdas's vars, in kirtan alongside the Guru's bani.

games.q: you're a scholar and a Persian poet, and you've come to the Guru. what do you do with your poetry?
o: give it up: devotion has no room for art.
turn it toward the Guru and the One.
keep it for the royal courts only.
games.why: Bhai Nand Lal kept writing in Persian, as Goya, and turned the whole art toward the Guru and the Divine.

practice: Find one short line from a poem first written in another language, Persian if you can, and read it once, then stay with it, noticing what the translator had to choose and what might have gone missing on the way across.
Then think of one gift you have, a skill, a craft, a language, and what it would look like turned toward something you love.
